title: Why Student Modeling Is So Important
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin explains why having a student demonstrate a task, routine, or procedure immediately after teacher modeling is a critical step in effective instruction. Having a peer replicate the teacher's example proves to the rest of the class that the task is achievable without help, removing potential excuses before they arise. Linsin notes this practice also sharpens the teacher's own performance, since they know the lesson's success depends on the selected student's execution. He weighs different approaches to selecting the student—always choosing a strong performer, deliberately choosing a struggling one, or ideally picking at random—arguing that unpredictability keeps every student engaged and attentive, since anyone might be called on. The piece closes with a broader claim that modeling, paired with student demonstration, should underlie the teaching of virtually every classroom task, transition, and routine.
points: Having a student demonstrate a task immediately after teacher modeling proves to the class that the task is achievable independently, removing potential excuses.
This practice also sharpens the teacher's own performance, since they know the lesson's success hinges on how well the chosen student executes it.
Linsin recommends selecting the demonstrating student unpredictably, ideally at random, so that every student stays attentive, not knowing if they'll be chosen.
An alternative for teachers not yet comfortable choosing randomly is to have multiple students model, either sequentially or as a group.
The broader claim is that modeling paired with student demonstration should underlie the teaching of virtually every classroom task, transition, and routine.
quotes: Modeling can be a uniquely powerful strategy. Which is why the most effective teachers rely on it more than any other method.
One of most critical steps to effective modeling is to select a student to follow your example, to mimic your moves down to the very last detail.
It proves to the rest of your class that it can be done. It proves that one of their own can perform the task, routine, or objective as well as the teacher—and without a stitch of help.
Asking a student to model immediately after you also keeps you sharp and at the top of your game.
The problem with both approaches is that if any one student realizes that they’re unlikely to be chosen, then it will affect their attentiveness.
No matter what you teach or what grade level, anything and everything you want your students to be able to do, should be modeled.
